subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Jupiter's Great Red Spot
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Jupiter's Great Red Spot.

hook.text: A storm larger than Earth has been raging on Jupiter for at least 350 years. It's the Great Red Spot.

buildup.text: Winds inside reach 680 km/h. The spot is an anticyclonic storm powered by Jupiter's internal heat.

discovery.text: First recorded in 1665, it has been continuously observed since the 1830s.

twist.text: The Great Red Spot is shrinking. In the 1800s it was three Earths wide. Now it's barely one.

climax.text: Why it has lasted centuries and why it's red remain open mysteries in planetary science.

punchline.text: A hurricane bigger than Earth. Centuries old. Still spinning.

quiz.question: What is happening to Jupiter's Great Red Spot over time?
options: It is slowly shrinking in size
It is growing larger and more intense
It is splitting into two separate storms

details.summary: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a massive anticyclonic storm larger than Earth, with wind speeds exceeding 400 km/h at its edges. It has been observed for at least 350 years and is the longest-known storm in the solar system.
details.whyItMatters: The Great Red Spot demonstrates that atmospheric dynamics on gas giants operate at scales and durations impossible on Earth. Understanding it helps scientists model weather systems on exoplanets and extreme atmospheric physics.
takeaways: The Great Red Spot is larger than Earth with 400+ km/h winds
It has persisted for at least 350 years of continuous observation
Recent data shows the storm is gradually shrinking over decades

faq.question: Why has the Great Red Spot lasted so long?
faq.answer: Jupiter has no solid surface to create friction and slow storms. The spot draws energy from Jupiter's internal heat and the jet streams flanking it. It also absorbs smaller storms that feed it energy.

faq.question: What makes the Great Red Spot red?
faq.answer: The exact cause is debated. Leading theories suggest ultraviolet sunlight breaks down chemicals (ammonia, acetylene, or phosphorus compounds) lofted to high altitudes in the storm, producing red-tinted compounds.
